I. A new Union Tribal Affairs Ministry policy framework is a reminder that India’s conservation
strategy is not a fortress conservation model but one in which protecting the country’s tigers is
a social contract. The policy’s foremost virtue is reiteration that people living near or inside
forests cannot be relocated until the Forest Rights Act (FRA) 2006 process has been completed,
affirming that they are stakeholders, not trespassers. This view has sadly been falling out of
favour with a government that is increasingly seeing forests solely for their climate utility and
a judiciary keen to settle long-standing disputes. The policy casting relocation as an
“exceptional” measure also overturns the 2024 National Tiger Conservation Authority directive
to remove villages en masse from tiger reserves. Instead of treating humans and tigers as
mutually exclusive, the framework promotes research and pilot projects on sustainable co-
habitation that could help redefine tiger conservation through a more socially legitimate, and
possibly more resilient model. Its invocation of the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act for
unlawful evictions and a three-tier system for redress also provide a safety net rarely available
to these communities.

This said, forest-dependent communities have varied needs: some expect hospitals and schools
while others fight to preserve traditional lifestyles. Equally, tigers are sensitive and the reason
many conservationists believe human-free core zones are essential to conserve apex predators.
A national mission to protect tigers on scientific terms needs to ensure such tracts.
Fundamentally, while a national policy protects rights, fine-grained mechanisms sensitive to
particular local conditions are crucial for people and tigers to sustainably coexist. Such
mechanisms are however beyond the ability of top-level Ministries. The conservation
establishment is likely to resist the new policy because it could slow efforts to consolidate tiger
habitats and increase the implementation burden, potentially leading to dual policies on the
ground. In fact, conservation in India is largely controlled by Forest Departments under the
Environment Ministry and States have wide latitude in implementing the FRA. Even in places
where local departments wield significant control, forced relocations may continue in States
that do not enforce the proposed National Framework for Community-Centred Conservation
and Relocation. While existing policy defines compensation criteria and the minimum inviolate
area for a sustainable population, their implementation often violates established principles.
Just as the fortress model has often been insensitive to people’s rights in practice, exiting it
should not mean entering one in which India’s natural riches can be forsworn.

indias-tigers/article70221403.ece

II. Have you ever slept through your alarm and had to skip breakfast? Have you ever wished
for more protein in the morning than what bland oatmeal could provide? Have you ever been
stranded in the woods, starving, with nothing but a raw egg? If you answered “yes” to at least
one of these questions, Lenny Livingston could have helped. You see, Lenny had a superpower.

…Well, it was less a superpower, and more a “specific issue resolver.”

Lenny Livingston could [insert drumroll here] fry an egg under any circumstances, provided
he had a frying pan handy. No, he couldn’t create fire to heat the pan. No, he didn’t have laser
vision to cook the egg. And, no, he didn’t switch the uncooked egg for a fried one when you
weren’t looking. He merely cracked the egg open, dropped it into the pan, and shook his fist at
it threateningly. Moments later, the egg was so perfectly fried, Gordan Ramsay himself would
call it “the most amazing” thing he’d ever eaten (before remarking the burnt toast that came
with it was “a real shame”). Then, one day, after frying an egg more from frustration than
because he was hungry, Lenny found a note in his pocket:

TOP SECRET! You are cordially invited to join The Super Pals @ 12 Chestnut Drive, 7pm
tonight. Knock three times. Tell no one.

How the note had gotten into Lenny’s pocket was a mystery. He’d been home all day and hadn’t
seen anyone. His pants were fresh out of the dryer. Clearly, whoever had put it there must have
had some great superpower, like invisibility or super speed! At 7pm, Lenny skipped all the way
to the noted address (a modest rowhome within the city) and knocked upon the door. An elderly
woman in a nightgown greeted him. Not exactly the guard he’d been expecting. “I’m here to
see The Super Pals,” Lenny whispered.

“Eh?” the woman said. “Speak up, sonny.”

Lenny cleared his throat. “The Super Pals.”

“There’s a gas station down the street,” she said. “They have a commode. First stop on the trail.
Restroom’s for customers only, though, so you’ll have to buy something.”

“Ma!” someone from within shouted. “Who is it?”

“Another pedestrian on the Pooper Trail, Steven. Never you mind. Go back to playing dragon
dungeons with your friends.”

“I’m here to join up,” Lenny called inside. “The Super Pals.”

There was a thunderous stamping up the steps. Steven – a greasy, heavy-set fellow – appeared
and pulled Lenny in. “Shh! What if someone heard you! Didn’t you read the note? Top secret!”

The woman groaned. “Fine. But wash your hands when you’re done. And don’t tell me you
always do. We’ll both know it’s a lie.”

III. Can a person be charged for trying to create discord between religious communities with
“unsaid words”? In a deeply troubling decision, the Allahabad High Court recently said that a
WhatsApp text can indeed give a “subtle message” to stoke interfaith strife, even without
explicitly mentioning religion. It refused to quash an FIR and directed the accused, Afaq
Ahmad, to face trial. The decision could have a chilling effect on free speech.

Ahmad had moved the HC after the Uttar Pradesh police had registered a case against him
under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita’s Section 352 — it criminalises intentional insults that
provoke a breach of public peace. The police had sought to incriminate Ahmad on the basis of
a WhatsApp text to two people. Ahmad’s lawyers argued that their client only intended to
convey resentment about his brother’s arrest. The HC, however, said that the Whatsapp text,
“definitely conveys an underlying and subtle message that his brother has been targeted in a
false case, because of his belonging to a particular religious community.” It went on to say,
“even if one were to think that no religious feelings of a class of citizens or community have
been outraged… it is certainly a message, which, by its unsaid words, is likely to create or
promote feelings of enmity, hatred and ill-will between religious communities… members of
a particular community, in the first instance, could think that they are being targeted by
members of another religious community by abusing the process of law”.

Criminal laws, especially those that deal with the fundamental Right to Freedom of Speech and
Expression, require a clinical interpretation. In looking for unsaid words and subtle messaging,
the HC seems to have gone against the Supreme Court’s landmark 2015 ruling in Shreya
Singhal v Union of India. The apex court had said that “a penal law is void for vagueness if it
fails to define the criminal offence with sufficient definiteness”. It had underlined that
“ordinary people should be able to understand what conduct is prohibited and what is
permitted”. The Allahabad HC verdict, in contrast, frames a vague unlawful zone that people
must steer clear of. It goes against Shreya Singhal’s strictures against the “arbitrary and
discriminatory enforcement of the law”. The HC must course correct.

SOURCE:https://indianexpress.com/article/opinion/editorials/discord-religious-communities-
unsaid-words-allahabad-hc-anti-free-speech-10328459/

V. Supreme Court has sought govt support to frame norms to compensate for wrongful arrest,
prosecution and conviction. It announced its intent as it overturned the conviction of a man on
death row for six years. SC has frequently acquitted death row convicts and expressed its anger
and distress at subpar and dishonest police work and prosecution. It has berated subordinate
courts for wrong judgments. SC’s intent is welcome but must be seen to completion. This gap
in our justice system has been discussed threadbare. The Law Commission made its
recommendations (2018) while a legislative attempt in Lok Sabha – a private member’s bill,
the Protection of Rights of Wrongful Convicts Bill (2019) – lapsed. BNS was an opportunity
missed to put a compensation framework for false arrests, detention and conviction on the
statute. Wrong imprisonment isn’t merely justice denied, but dignity destroyed, lives shattered
and faith in justice system irreparably damaged.

So, how should compensation be decided? Law Commission recommended considering the
offence’s seriousness, severity of punishment, length of detention, damage to health, harm to
reputation, and of course, loss of income and opportunities. Add legal fees. In 2014, New York
City paid $40mn to five black and Latino men wrongly convicted in their teens in 1989 for a
brutal attack on a NY jogger in Central Park. DNA forensics cleared them 25 years later. US’s
National Registry of Exonerations recorded 153 exonerations in 2023, of which “nearly 84%
were people of colour”, and who “lost 2,230 years collectively for crimes they did not
commit…” Between 1989, when the state-wise record was started, and 2023, New York state
had made a total payout of $322mn to those wrongfully incarcerated.

India does not even maintain a record of wrongful arrests, prosecutions or convictions. And
when compensation is provided, the amount is often paltry. Discharged in 1996, it took Isro
scientist Nambi Narayanan 20 years to win a compensation of ₹50L. SC said state can’t avoid
its “vicarious liability”. But in 1998, SC had awarded him ₹1L in damages. One is expected to
be simply grateful one’s free, even if broken and shattered.

VI. The recent surrender of a senior Maoist figure known as Devuji has drawn renewed
attention to India’s long-running Left-Wing Extremism (LWE) challenge. Security agencies
have described the development as part of a broader pattern of declining insurgent capacity,
attributed to coordinated operations, infrastructure expansion, and targeted rehabilitation
policies. Government officials emphasize that surrender frameworks combine financial
incentives, vocational training, and reintegration measures aimed at encouraging militants to
abandon armed struggle. Analysts, however, caution that ideological networks and localized
grievances continue to sustain pockets of insurgency across certain forested and mineral-rich
regions. The episode highlights the evolving nature of counter-insurgency policy in India,
which increasingly integrates security responses with developmental initiatives. Experts
suggest that long-term resolution depends not only on tactical success but also on addressing
governance deficits, land rights disputes, and socio-economic disparities in affected districts.

X. The foundational legal maxim Nemo Iudex In Causa Sua, which holds that no person shall
be a judge in their own cause, constitutes a cardinal principle of natural justice and a bedrock

its profound utility lies in its equal commitment to safeguarding the perception of fairness,
thereby maintaining public confidence in the judicial system. The principle operates not merely
to root out actual bias but to eliminate any reasonable suspicion thereof, recognizing that justice
must be seen to be done.

The application of this rule encompasses several distinct yet interrelated doctrines. Bias is
categorized as either actual, requiring direct proof of prejudice, or apparent, governed by the
pervasive “reasonable suspicion” test. This objective test inquires whether a fair-minded and
informed observer, apprised of all relevant circumstances, would perceive a real possibility of
bias. Grounds giving rise to such a suspicion are well-established and include any financial or
proprietary interest in the outcome, however minimal; personal relationships suggesting
friendship or animosity; prior involvement in the same matter as an advocate or investigator;
and institutional biases where a decision-maker has pre-judged the issue. The maxim’s reach
extends beyond the traditional judiciary to all public decision-makers, including administrative
tribunals and regulators, where prior public advocacy for a specific outcome may vitiate
impartiality.

To operationalize the principle, legal systems have developed rules for judicial recusal or
disqualification, whereby a judge must—or may be required to—step aside from proceedings.
Importantly, the right to an unbiased tribunal can be waived by a party provided such waiver
is informed and unequivocal. Ultimately, this maxim is not a mere procedural technicality but
a constitutive element of a legitimate legal order. It assures citizens that decisions affecting
their rights are made by neutral arbiters, free from personal interest or preconception. In so

XII. The Indian Penal Code, 1860, designates offences against the state’s very existence as its
most severe crimes, encapsulated in Chapter VI. At its apex lies Section 121, which
criminalizes the act of waging, attempting to wage, or abetting the waging of war against the
Government of India. This provision targets not mere disorder but collective violence of a
political character aimed at overthrowing the government or coercing it by force. The essence
of "waging war" distinguishes it from riots or isolated rebellions; it requires an assembly with
a public, general purpose and a force sufficient to challenge the state’s sovereignty. An
illustrative example is an armed insurrection to seize a government arsenal with the goal of
subverting constitutional authority. Given its gravity, the punishment is extraordinarily
stringent: death or imprisonment for life, coupled with a fine and mandatory forfeiture of
property.

Recognizing that the gravest threats often begin in secret, the law proactively targets conspiracy
through Section 121A. This section penalizes the very agreement to commit offences under
Section 121, criminalizing the planning stage before any overt act of violence materializes. The
key ingredient is a conspiracy between two or more persons either to wage war or to deprive
India of its sovereignty. Thus, the state need not wait for an uprising; the plot itself is punishable
by imprisonment for life or up to ten years, and a fine.

Further along the continuum of preparation, Section 122 addresses the tangible steps taken
towards this end. It punishes collecting arms, ammunition, or otherwise preparing to wage war,
provided such acts are done with the specific intention of using them against the state. This
moves beyond conspiracy into actionable preparation, meriting a similarly severe punishment
of life imprisonment or up to ten years, and a fine.

Finally, Section 123 casts a wide net by criminalizing the concealment of a design to wage war.
An individual who, knowing of such a treasonous design, actively conceals it with the intent
to facilitate its execution, becomes complicit. This offence underscores the legal duty not to
aid such plots through silence or deception, punishable by imprisonment up to ten years and a
fine.

Collectively, these sections form a formidable legal bulwark. They protect state stability by
addressing the entire spectrum of treasonous activity—from the ultimate act of war, through
its conspiracy and preparation, down to its intentional concealment—ensuring that both action
and treacherous intent are met with the full force of the law.

XIV. Judicial review of administrative action constitutes the cornerstone of India’s
constitutional framework for ensuring governmental accountability and upholding the rule of
law. As the core mechanism to check administrative excesses, it empowers constitutional courts
to scrutinize the legality, rationality, and procedural propriety of executive decisions. This
supervisory jurisdiction, inherent under Articles 32 and 226 of the Constitution, is not an appeal
on merits but a review of the decision-making process itself, ensuring that state power is
exercised within defined legal boundaries.

The grounds for such review are well-established. Firstly, jurisdictional error occurs when an
authority acts without jurisdiction, in excess of it, or fails to exercise a jurisdiction it possesses.
Secondly, an error of law apparent on the face of the record allows courts to intervene where a
clear legal flaw is discernible from the order itself, without delving into intricate evidence.
Thirdly, while factual findings are typically respected, courts will intervene in cases of an error
in finding of fact where the conclusion is so perverse that no reasonable person could have
arrived at it, or is based on no evidence whatsoever.

The principles of natural justice—audi alteram partem (hear the other side) and nemo judex in
causa sua (no one should be a judge in their own cause)—form a vital ground. Any decision
violating these foundational tenets of fairness, such as acting with bias or denying a reasonable
hearing, is rendered void. Furthermore, abuse or misuse of discretion is a critical check against
arbitrariness. Discretion must be exercised reasonably, for the purpose granted, without mala
fides, and considering all relevant factors; its misuse on irrelevant grounds or in a manifestly
unfair manner invites judicial correction. Finally, procedural ultra vires ensures that mandatory
statutory procedures are meticulously followed, as their breach invalidates the subsequent
action.

Thus, judicial review operates as an essential democratic safeguard. It balances administrative
efficiency with individual rights, ensuring that public power is exercised in a manner that is
neither beyond authority nor contrary to justice, thereby reinforcing constitutional governance.
